Read CPU quota utilisation, memory against the runtime container's own cgroup
limit, and disk usage for the workspace mount, straight from the runtime
container's cgroup v2 accounting and a statfs of the workspace mount.

No metrics-server is required: this works on clusters where `kubectl top`
reports "Metrics API not available", which is every local (orbstack/k3s-style)
cluster. Memory is reported against the container's own limit (current usage,
the peak high-water mark, and a real OOM-kill count from the cgroup, replacing
a post-mortem guess); CPU utilisation is measured against its quota over a
sample interval. A named warning fires when memory, memory's peak, or disk
usage cross a fixed threshold; the memory-peak and OOM-kill warnings also
consult the environment's retained history, because those cgroup counters
reset when the container restarts and an environment that has been
OOM-killed would otherwise read as memory-healthy. Every field reports its own unavailability
(cgroup v1, an unlimited limit, a file that could not be read) rather than
failing the call, since those are normal on some clusters, not errors.

Disk is reported for the whole mount (node, shared): every environment
scheduled on the same node sees the identical total/used/percent, so cleaning
up one environment may barely move it. The own-usage line beneath it (a `du`
of this environment's own directory) is the figure this environment can
actually act on.

On a build-capable environment (local-agent, remote-agent), every image build
actually runs in the erun-dind sidecar, a separate cgroup from the runtime
container above -- so this command also reads the sidecar's own CPU and
memory against its own limit and reports it alongside, with the same named
warnings if the sidecar itself nears its memory limit or records an OOM kill.
A busy build no longer reads as an idle environment. If the sidecar's own
cgroup could not be read, the output says so instead; `erun observe` reports
its resource limits either way.

The environment's standing sizing recommendation rides along with the reading
whenever the usage history behind it can be read: it is derived from history
the environment's own pod monitor retained, which lives with the environment.
Which surfaces show it follows from that, not from which command was run:
the `usage` and `resize` tools over the environment's MCP endpoint and
`erun list`'s `runtime-pod:` block all resolve the same recommendation from
the same evidence, so no two of them can disagree. A host that has never
monitored the environment has no history to resolve, and reports the reading
with no sizing verdict at all rather than a zero-value one.

Usage:
  erun usage [flags]

Examples:
  erun usage --tenant team --environment dev
  erun usage --tenant team --environment dev --interval 3 --output json

Flags:
      --dry-run              Resolve and trace mutating actions without executing them.
      --environment string   Target a specific environment; requires --tenant
  -h, --help                 help for usage
      --interval float       CPU sample window in seconds, clamped to 0.1-30: usage is read, the window elapses, then it is read again so utilisation is a rate rather than a cumulative counter (default 1)
      --tenant string        Target a specific tenant (default: the current scope)

Global Flags:
      --output string   Result format: text (default, human stream) or json (structured result on stdout for orchestrators). (default "text")
      --time            Print the elapsed runtime after the command finishes.
  -v, --verbose count   Increase verbosity: -v streams external tool output, -vv adds erun command traces.
